claims.text: The maintenance of structural and chemical stability in initially random-solid-solution multimetal nanoparticles is governed by the balance between configurational entropy and atomic-diffusion kinetics.
A solid solution is maintained when kinetic barriers to atomic reordering remain high relative to the thermodynamic drive for ordering or phase separation.
Increasing temperature can enhance atomic mobility sufficiently to overcome kinetic barriers to reordering.
Enhanced atomic mobility can enable local chemical ordering or clustering.
Local ordering or clustering degrades the initially homogeneous solid-solution structure.
The initial material consists of nanoparticles containing five or more metals in near-equiatomic ratios and crystallized as a disordered solid solution.
Local atomic diffusion and the resulting tendency toward short-range ordering or clustering mediate the effect of temperature on phase stability.
At lower temperatures, high configurational entropy stabilizes the disordered solid solution despite a small thermodynamic drive for ordering.
At higher temperatures, enhanced atomic mobility lowers or overcomes the kinetic barrier to diffusion.
Atoms can form ordered or chemically segregated clusters when the enthalpic gain from reconfiguration overcomes entropic stabilization.
Competition among configurational entropy, enthalpic driving forces, and diffusion kinetics determines whether the nanoparticles depart from their initial homogeneous phase.
A controlled inert or process-relevant atmosphere can minimize oxidation and other extrinsic influences during thermal exposure.
When kinetic barriers remain effective, the nanoparticles will retain their solid-solution structure with minimal short-range ordering.
At sufficiently high temperature, increased atomic mobility will produce more chemical clustering or local ordering than is present in the initial baseline.
Changes in alloy composition can alter the stable phase or structural configuration of a multicomponent alloy.
Nanoparticle surface effects may modify atomic-diffusion kinetics and the temperature-dependent stability response relative to bulk alloys.
XRD, TEM, atom-probe analysis, and compositional mapping can be used to assess phase changes, local ordering, clustering, and phase separation after annealing.
A lack of any statistically significant increase in ordering or clustering over 473–1923 K would falsify the proposed temperature-driven-mobility mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis explicitly permits retention of the solid solution whenever kinetic barriers remain effective and states that the transition temperature may be unknown. Therefore, observing no ordering anywhere in the tested range can be explained by persistent barriers or a transition outside the accessible conditions and is not, by itself, a decisive falsification as claimed.
